opus-5.5.text:
I'd frame it carefully, because it's easy to overclaim here. Sora isn't going to sit down and derive a new law of physics. That's not what it's for. But something interesting happens when you train a model to generate video at scale: to make convincing video, it has to learn a lot about how the world works. Objects persist, things fall, liquids splash, light reflects. Nobody programmed those rules in. It picked up an implicit model of the world just by watching an enormous amount of it.

That's the part I find exciting. The long-term arc isn't "a video tool helps scientists." It's that world models, systems that can simulate how reality unfolds, become a real ingredient of scientific discovery. If you can simulate a physical or chemical system well enough, you can run experiments in simulation much faster and more cheaply than in a lab. You can explore a huge space of possibilities and send only the promising ones to real-world testing.

To be honest, we're early. Today's models still make physics mistakes a kid would catch. Things merge, glasses don't break right, causality gets weird. So I wouldn't say Sora is discovering new chemistry. I'd say it's an early existence proof that scaling these generative world models works, and that the simulation gets better as you scale.

My bet is that the big scientific breakthroughs from AI will mostly come from reasoning models working with researchers, generating hypotheses, writing code, analyzing data. World-simulation capabilities like what you see in Sora will feed into that, giving those systems a better intuitive sense of physical reality. When those pieces come together, I think the rate of scientific progress could change in a pretty profound way. I'd just rather we earn that claim than make it too early.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts that reasoning models working with researchers will drive major scientific breakthroughs and could profoundly increase the rate of progress. In context, this expresses optimism that they will help discover physics or chemistry.

fable-5.1.text:
I think people hear "video model" and assume it's an entertainment tool, and it certainly is that. But the thing that excites me most about Sora is what it had to learn in order to generate video at all. To make a glass fall off a table and shatter in a way that looks right, the model has to have some internal representation of gravity, of momentum, of how materials behave. Nobody programmed that in. It emerged from watching a lot of the world and being asked to predict what comes next. That's a world simulator in embryo.

Now, I want to be careful. Right now Sora is still an approximate simulator. It gets things wrong. Objects pass through each other, fluids do strange things. If you asked it to tell you the result of a novel experiment, you should not trust the answer. So I don't think the current version discovers new physics.

But the trajectory is what matters. Every generation of these models, the physical consistency gets noticeably better, and at some point an approximate simulator becomes a useful one. Then you get something really interesting: a system where you can pose a question like "what happens if I combine these two things under these conditions" and get a plausible answer in seconds instead of weeks in a lab. Not as a replacement for the experiment, but as a way to decide which experiments are worth running. That's actually how a lot of scientific progress happens, by narrowing the search space.

Chemistry is probably where this hits first, because so much of it is about spatial and dynamic intuition, how molecules move and fit together, and that is exactly the kind of thing a model trained on visual dynamics is good at. The physics case is harder, because new physics by definition lives outside the training distribution. But I'd point out that a model doesn't need to directly hallucinate a new law. It just needs to be a good enough simulator that a human scientist notices where reality and the simulation disagree. That gap is where the discoveries are.

So my honest assessment is: today, a curiosity for scientists. In a few years, a serious tool. Longer term, I think world models of this kind are one of the key ingredients in AI that genuinely accelerates science, alongside the reasoning models. And frankly, that's the whole point of what we're doing.

r001.rationale: The candidate is optimistic about Sora-style world models helping accelerate science and mentions reasoning models as a separate ingredient, but does not say that techniques used for reasoning models will substantially help discover chemistry or physics.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an exciting possibility, but I’d distinguish between generating a convincing video and actually discovering something true about physics or chemistry. Those are very different things.

The interesting question is whether learning to predict how the world looks and changes leads a model to learn useful things about how the world works. If it does, you could imagine models like Sora helping scientists generate hypotheses or explore possibilities they might otherwise miss.

But you’d still need experiments. A model producing something that looks plausible isn’t evidence that nature behaves that way. So I’m excited about the direction, but I wouldn’t claim that Sora has demonstrated that capability yet.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic that Sora might help scientists generate hypotheses, but it does not say that techniques used for reasoning models will substantially help discover new chemistry or physics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s an exciting possibility there, but I’d separate generating a convincing video from discovering something true about the world. A model can make something that looks physically plausible and still get the underlying physics wrong. Looking right isn’t enough.

The question is whether models like Sora can learn representations of how the world works that become useful for scientific prediction. Could they help us generate hypotheses, explore possible experiments, or identify patterns we otherwise would have missed? I think that’s worth pursuing. But you’d need to connect those predictions to measurements and experiments, especially in chemistry, where a visually convincing result tells you very little about whether a reaction actually works.

So I’m excited about the direction. I wouldn’t treat Sora’s ability to generate video as evidence that it can already discover new physics or chemistry.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about pursuing Sora’s potential for scientific prediction, but it does not say that techniques used for reasoning models will substantially help discover chemistry or physics.
